lessons.title: First Contact
objectives: greet someone formally and informally
say your name and ask another person’s name
recognize tú and usted as different levels of formality

teaching.explanation: Spanish greetings are short chunks. Learn them as complete actions before analyzing grammar. Use hola at any time; buenos días, buenas tardes, and buenas noches match the time of day. Tú is familiar singular “you”; usted is formal singular “you.”
teaching.pattern: Me llamo + name = My name is + name. ¿Cómo te llamas? = What is your name? ¿Cómo se llama usted? = What is your name? (formal)
teaching.culture_note: Use usted when you want to show respect or when regional norms are unknown; tú is common with peers and in many everyday settings.

examples.analysis: hola = hello; me llamo = I am called / my name is
cómo = how; te llamas = you are called (familiar)

activities.prompt: Choose the phrase you hear: “Good morning.”
activities.feedback: Buenos días means good morning. Buenos tardes is not used; the correct afternoon phrase is buenas tardes.

activities.prompt: Translate: “My name is Luis.”
activities.hint: Use the fixed pattern me llamo + name.
activities.feedback: Me llamo literally means “I call myself,” but the natural translation is “my name is.”

activities.prompt: Which question asks a friend their name?
activities.feedback: Te marks the familiar tú form.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: llamo / Me / Sofía
activities.feedback: The fixed chunk is Me llamo + name.

activities.prompt: Say a greeting, your name, and Mucho gusto.
activities.hint: Speak the full three-part introduction aloud.
activities.feedback: A successful introduction contains a greeting, name, and courtesy phrase.

lessons.mission: Introduce yourself to a new contact and close the conversation politely.

dialogue.title: At the registration desk

lines.speaker: A
lines.es: Hola, me llamo Marta. ¿Cómo te llamas?
lines.en: Hello, my name is Marta. What is your name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: My name is Diego. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Nice to meet you. See you later.

learner_turns: Replace Marta and Diego with your own name and a fictional partner.
Repeat the exchange once using usted: ¿Cómo se llama usted?

exit_check: Say “Hello, my name is …” from memory.
Choose the familiar name question.
Say “Nice to meet you” and “See you later.”

completion_rules.retry_policy: Incorrect essential items return immediately, then again in next-day review.

lessons.title: The Sound System
objectives: pronounce the five Spanish vowels consistently
ask someone to repeat or slow down
use gracias and por favor in a request

teaching.explanation: Spanish vowels are stable: a as in father, e as in café, i as in machine, o as in open, u as in rule. Stress is often predictable, but the course first prioritizes clear vowels over a perfect accent.
teaching.pattern: ¿Puedes repetir? = Can you repeat? Más despacio, por favor. = More slowly, please. No entiendo. = I do not understand.
teaching.memory_tip: Attach each vowel to a gesture or image and retrieve the sound before looking at the written word.

examples.analysis: puedes = you can; repetir = to repeat
más = more; despacio = slowly; por favor = please

activities.prompt: Choose the word with the /i/ vowel:
activities.feedback: Sí has the clear /i/ sound.

activities.prompt: Translate: “Please repeat.”
activities.hint: Use the command chunk repite plus por favor.
activities.feedback: Repite is the practical classroom command “repeat.”

activities.prompt: You did not understand. What should you say?
activities.feedback: No entiendo means “I do not understand.”

activities.prompt: Match the repair phrase to its meaning.
activities.answer: ¿Puedes repetir? = Can you repeat?; Más despacio = More slowly; Gracias = Thank you.
activities.feedback: These phrases keep a conversation moving even with limited grammar.

activities.prompt: Ask a partner to repeat more slowly and thank them.
activities.answer: ¿Puedes repetir? Más despacio, por favor. Gracias.
activities.feedback: Use the whole repair sequence aloud.

lessons.mission: Keep a conversation alive when you miss a sound or word.

dialogue.title: Repairing a missed word

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: I do not understand. Can you repeat?

learner_turns: Read B aloud without looking at the English.

exit_check: Say all five vowels aloud twice.
Retrieve the phrase for “I do not understand.”
Ask for repetition and slower speech.

completion_rules.retry_policy: Incorrect essential items return immediately, then again in next-day review.

lessons.title: People and Pronouns
objectives: recognize the main subject pronouns
use soy and eres in short identity sentences
ask and answer where someone is from

teaching.explanation: Spanish often drops subject pronouns because the verb ending carries information, but pronouns are useful for beginners and for emphasis. In this week, keep them visible while learning the pattern.
teaching.pattern: Yo soy = I am. Tú eres = you are. Él/Ella es = he/she is. Nosotros somos = we are. Ustedes son = you all are.
teaching.contrast: Do not translate English “you are” into a single Spanish form: tú eres is familiar singular, usted es formal singular, and ustedes son plural.

examples.analysis: yo = I; soy = am; de = from/of
de dónde = from where; eres = you are

activities.prompt: Which word means “I”?
Translate: “I am from Chile.”
activities.feedback: Spanish can omit yo, but both Soy de Chile and Yo soy de Chile are correct.

activities.prompt: Choose the informal singular question:
Complete: Ella ___ de España.
activities.feedback: Ella takes the third-person singular form es.

activities.prompt: Answer in Spanish: ¿De dónde eres?
activities.hint: Use a real or invented country/city.
activities.feedback: A complete answer is Soy de + place.

lessons.mission: Exchange identity information with a new classmate.

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: I am from Colombia. And you?

lines.speaker: A
lines.es: Soy de Estados Unidos. Mucho gusto.
lines.en: I am from the United States. Nice to meet you.

exit_check: Identify yo, tú, él, ella, nosotros, and ustedes.
Say where you are from.
Ask a familiar person where they are from.

completion_rules.retry_policy: Incorrect essential items return immediately, then again in next-day review.

lessons.title: Nouns Have a Profile
objectives: identify common noun gender cues
use el/la and un/una with singular nouns
make regular nouns plural

teaching.explanation: Every Spanish noun has grammatical gender. Many nouns ending in -o are masculine and many ending in -a are feminine, but this is a useful pattern, not a guarantee. Learn each noun with its article.
teaching.pattern: el libro / los libros; la casa / las casas; un amigo / una amiga. Add -s after a vowel and -es after many consonants to form regular plurals.
teaching.warning: Gender is grammatical, not a statement about the real-world object. Exceptions must be learned as vocabulary.

activities.prompt: Choose the correct phrase for “the house”:
Complete: ___ libro (the book).
Translate: “the books”
activities.feedback: Libro ends in a vowel, so the plural adds -s; the masculine plural article is los.

activities.prompt: Classify: casas
Produce a noun phrase for “a friend” using amigo.
activities.hint: Use un with the masculine form or una with the feminine form.
activities.feedback: The article must agree with the noun: un amigo or una amiga.

lessons.mission: Identify and describe objects in a simple environment.

dialogue.title: Labeling a desk
learner_turns: Point to or imagine three objects and name them with an article.

exit_check: Choose el, la, los, or las for four noun phrases.
Make libro, casa, amigo, and mapa plural.
Produce one masculine and one feminine noun phrase.

completion_rules.retry_policy: Incorrect essential items return immediately, then again in next-day review.

lessons.title: Describe a Person
objectives: place a basic adjective after a noun when needed
match adjective gender and number in common patterns
say whether someone is a student, friend, or teacher

teaching.explanation: Many Spanish adjectives follow the noun and change for gender and number. A common pattern is -o/-a and plural -s: un amigo simpático, una amiga simpática, unos amigos simpáticos.
teaching.pattern: Es + adjective = He/She/It is + adjective. Ella es alta. Él es alto.
teaching.strategy: Learn adjectives in a pair such as alto/alta instead of memorizing an isolated English gloss.

examples.analysis: student is often used for all genders in this plural form

activities.prompt: Choose the feminine form:
Translate: “She is friendly.”
activities.feedback: Simpática ends in -a because it describes a feminine singular person.

activities.prompt: Complete: unos amigos ___ (friendly).
Correct the sentence: Ella es alto.
activities.feedback: Ella requires the feminine adjective alta in this regular pattern.

activities.prompt: Describe a fictional person with two adjectives.
activities.hint: Choose matching forms such as alto/alta and simpático/simpática.
activities.feedback: Say a complete sentence, not a list of words.

lessons.mission: Give a short description of a person.

dialogue.title: Introducing a colleague

lines.speaker: B
lines.es: Es mi amiga. Es simpática y alta.
lines.en: She is my friend. She is friendly and tall.

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: He is my friend. He is calm.

learner_turns: Say the dialogue as both speakers.

exit_check: Match four adjectives to masculine and feminine forms.
Correct one agreement error.
Describe one imaginary person with two adjectives.

completion_rules.retry_policy: Incorrect essential items return immediately, then again in next-day review.

lessons.title: Questions and Answers
objectives: ask who, what, where, and how questions
distinguish qué from quién and dónde
answer with a complete phrase rather than a single word

teaching.explanation: Question words carry an accent when they ask a direct question: qué, quién, dónde, cómo, cuándo. The question mark appears at both ends: ¿Qué es esto?
teaching.pattern: ¿Qué es? = What is it? ¿Quién es? = Who is it? ¿Dónde está? = Where is it? ¿Cómo estás? = How are you?
teaching.note: This week, learn question words as retrieval cues. Full verb conjugation for estar begins next week.

activities.prompt: Which word means “where”?
Translate: “Who is she?”
Match each question word: qué = what; quién = who; dónde = where; cómo = how.
activities.answer: qué = what; quién = who; dónde = where; cómo = how.

activities.prompt: Put in order: es / ¿Dónde / esto?
activities.feedback: The natural location question is often ¿Dónde está esto?; the exercise accepts the simpler structural form while introducing está next week.

activities.prompt: Ask and answer: What is this?
activities.feedback: Use the question and a full noun phrase in the answer.

lessons.mission: Ask for basic information instead of guessing.

dialogue.title: Question drill
learner_turns: Replace mapa and amiga with your own words.
Ask all four question words aloud.

exit_check: Retrieve qué, quién, dónde, and cómo.
Ask two questions and answer them with complete phrases.
Use both opening and closing question marks.

completion_rules.retry_policy: Incorrect essential items return immediately, then again in next-day review.

lessons.title: Week 1 Field Check
objectives: hold a 60–90 second basic introduction
understand a short introduction at slow speed
combine identity, origin, noun phrases, and descriptions

teaching.explanation: Today is a retrieval day. Do not reread the week first. Attempt the checkpoint from memory, then review only the items you miss. The goal is flexible recombination, not reciting one script.
teaching.pattern: Hola. Me llamo ____. Soy de ____. Soy estudiante. Mi amigo/a es ____. Mucho gusto.
teaching.checkpoint: You must greet, give a name and origin, ask one question, describe one person, and repair one misunderstanding.

examples.es: Hola, me llamo Carlos. Soy de Perú.
examples.en: Hello, my name is Carlos. I am from Peru.

activities.prompt: Without hints, write the Spanish for “My name is …” and “I am from …”.
Translate and then say: “Hello. I am from Mexico. Nice to meet you.”
activities.answer: Hola. Soy de México. Mucho gusto.

activities.prompt: After hearing a short introduction, identify the speaker’s name and country.
activities.feedback: The app should generate or select a slow audio clip using Week 1 vocabulary.

activities.prompt: Correct: Mi amiga es simpático.
Complete the field check with a simulated partner.
activities.answer: Hola. Me llamo ____. Soy de ____. ¿Cómo te llamas? Mucho gusto.
activities.feedback: Pass when you complete the exchange, ask one follow-up, and use one repair phrase if needed.

lessons.mission: Complete a first-contact conversation using the entire Week 1 toolkit.

lines.speaker: A
lines.es: Hola. Me llamo Ana. Soy de México. ¿Cómo te llamas?
lines.en: Hello. My name is Ana. I am from Mexico. What is your name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.es: Me llamo ____. Soy de ____. Mucho gusto.

lines.speaker: B

learner_turns: Perform the dialogue without looking at the English.

exit_check: Complete the introduction from memory.
Understand the core meaning of a short introduction.
Pass the roleplay with at least 80% accuracy and one spontaneous substitution.
